speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It was reported that Singapore could have been a target.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Essentially, if they had been directed to attack in Singapore, they would have attacked.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The threat of terrorism is real and the battle against it is for every Singaporean to bear.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Being vigilant against an attack and staying united for an attack vest on our shores is key.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If we stay united as one people, we will be successful in denying any terrorist his victory.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We are very fortunate to have a dedicated, professional and reliable Home Team.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That Home Team is a key pillar in our battle against terrorism, but it is not a fight for that team to bear alone.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singaporeans must play their part alongside dedicated Home Team officers to keep vigilant against terror threats.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such threats come in many forms ‒ acts of actual violence, radical ideology preaching discord, funding of terror cells or glorification through the Internet of senseless causes.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Couple all of that with the trend around the world, in which governments start to look inward and become fervently nationalistic.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These trends and movements could fuel further global discord among peoples of different cultures and ethnicity.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore and Singaporeans must resist these negative global trends and tides and never allow them to envelope Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Thankfully, through initiatives, such as the ethnic integration programme in public housing and Racial Harmony Day, the different cultures and ethnic groups in Singapore are able to enjoy harmonious relationships.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Nevertheless, we must continue to work at it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because in multiracial societies, where peoples of different creeds and races intermingle, the risk of flashpoints is higher.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore is no exception, and we have to be careful when we encounter incidents which may become potential flashpoints.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It was assuring to read in that same report that the Islamic Religious Council of Singapore (MUIS) took the courageous and generous position when it stated that, "MUIS takes a serious view of any behaviour or speech which promotes feelings of enmity, hatred or ill-will among different faith communities." What we have attained, what we have enjoyed, we need to maintain, nurture and strengthen.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Furthermore, one, how can we carefully manage potential flashpoints?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How can we carefully manage potential flashpoint incidents and strengthen our racial and religious harmony which is vital to Singapore in peacetime as well as in the aftermath of a terrorist attack?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Also, how is MHA ensuring Singaporeans continue to welcome globalisation instead of turning isolationist, since we all know an isolationist Singapore will lead to her severe detriment.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Let us strengthen our fight against terrorism and let us stand together with our dedicated Home Team in this collective fight against those who seek to do us harm.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We need to be vigilant so that, as a society, we are ready for whatever comes our way ‒ leaders, public servants, citizens standing together as one.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can the Ministry update us on the threat situation internationally, regionally, domestically?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We also need to actively study the new and innovative terror tactics that we are reading about around the world, so that we can learn how best to counter them.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Tactics that are using household items, such as knives, tactics that use easily available equipment and vehicles as weapons.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Likewise, we also need to protect our society from self-radicalisation, especially with the proliferation of online recruitment, extremist propaganda and social media tactics.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Looking to our landscape, we are densely populated.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Many of these population centres are in our Housing and Development Board (HDB) heartlands.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: All these pose unique challenges for rapid responses against a terrorist attack.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can MHA update us on how we are upgrading our counterterror efforts and how we are enhancing Home Team capabilities and SGSecure so that, as a whole of society, we are equipped to deter and, if needed, respond?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Since we launched the SGSecure movement last year, can MHA share the progress of its outreach efforts, in particular, in the community as well as in workplaces?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I urge MHA to work with the community and businesses to recruit SGSecure Ambassadors at every HDB block and at every workplace.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: These ambassadors can help spread the SGSecure message and be trained in first aid, automated external defibrillators (AED) and skills to handle the community or workplace response in the event of a terrorist attack, especially the day after.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In fact, the first training session starts in a fortnight.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I hope MHA can give full support through funding the training, exercises and our outreach to the residents and community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: From my conversations with people, there appears to be an increased awareness of SGSecure.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is important to ensure that everyone remains vigilant and aware of what needs to be done in the event of a terror attack.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I, therefore, would like to know the update on the implementation of SGSecure.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Are there means to measure the level of awareness and preparedness of the community?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I note grassroots and community leaders are being trained to equip them with the knowledge and skills to handle a terror crisis.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Multiracial and multi-religious sensitivities may arise and community leaders play an important role to ensure that the community stays strong and united.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I was fortunate to observe these exercises and would like to highlight the following.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Perhaps, there could be better coordination of what is to be done by the different groups on the ground.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Two, the information on the community networks that can be relied on to provide support during times of emergency was not updated.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Following from the exercises, the community leaders were asked to continue building and updating their networks within their local communities.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It would be useful to provide them with specific guidance on how they should go about doing this.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Three, there were queries on the chain of command and the extent to which the community can take initiatives.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Perhaps, more resolution can be given in future trainings.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe coordination of the exercises can be improved.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: On the issue of multiracial and multi-religious sensitivities which I spoke about earlier, like Mr de Souza, I also read about the recent case where an imam was alleged to have made offensive remarks about Christians and Jews, and we have seen reactions from netizens.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Would the Ministry be able to give information on this case?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I fully support the mandatory annual security exercise that was introduced in 2009 to ensure higher standards of security requirement can be maintained.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: That said, I would like to ask the Minister for Home Affairs whether a review could be done on this annual grading exercise.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Could MHA provide clearer guidelines and share the benchmarking process used in the assessment?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some agencies risk losing their right to secure a site because their grading slipped a notch.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The officers consequently will either have to change employers to stay on the same site or have to relocate to another site, all of which create considerable constraints.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We hope MHA or PLRD can review this as well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The need for additional resources for policing is clear.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: More people mean a higher population density, increased interaction and proximity, more potential for crime and more assets to protect.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Over the last few decades, the role of the Auxiliary Police has expanded exponentially.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: From an initial brief of static guarding of key installations to accompanying cash in transit, the Auxiliary Police are now in roles that require them to interact with the public in a variety of scenarios, such as crowd control, management of prisoners, checkpoint security and policing liquor control zones.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The training of the Auxiliary Police has been enhanced, but is it adequate to ensure that the Auxiliary Police Officers (APOs) are equipped to meet the challenging needs of handling complex and unpredictable situations?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Policing Singapore is complicated by the fact that our population consists of 1.7 million non-resident foreigners.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I wonder whether the shortage will lead to a compromise in recruitment standards.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Several Singaporeans have expressed to me their concern about foreign APOs walking around with firearms.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Related concerns also crossed my mind, in particular, in the wake of the Little India riots in 2013, when it was clear from the incident reports that quite a number of the APOs at the scene were not Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What security risk is posed by having foreign APOs carrying firearms?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Is it time to consider arming APOs, especially fresh recruits from overseas, with less lethal weapons, such as stun guns?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Next, I move on to safeguards during Police investigations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At the same time, the criminal justice system needs to balance state power with due process and ensure that investigations are conducted lawfully, with suspects accorded their constitutional and legal rights.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One of the safeguards proposed by myself and others during previous Committee of Supply (COS) debates was to video-record the process of the recording of statements from suspects.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As argued previously, such a procedure will also save the state from spending time to address frivolous challenges in Court and protect officers from false allegations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Ministry had indicated that it would do a pilot project in the first quarter of 2016.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Could the Minister elaborate on the rationale and when we can expect the pilot to commence?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Article 9 of the Constitution guarantees the right to consult the legal practitioner to a person under arrest, but case law has held that this right is subject to the exigencies of Police investigations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: During the COS debate 10 years ago, in 2007, there was a pilot announced to give early access to counsel.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In some cases, the individual under investigation may suffer in his ability to earn a livelihood while the investigation continues, for example, when a person's vocational licence to be a public bus or taxi driver is suspended or revoked during the pendency of investigations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Sometimes, cases hang for months with no visible investigative step being taken.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This leaves the accused person in indefinite limbo and unable to earn a living.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Could there be a monitoring mechanism to ensure that such cases are investigated with a certain haste?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Singapore has acceded to the Convention of the Rights of the Child (CRC).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is one of the few human rights treaties that Singapore has acceded to, showing the importance our country places on this set of international obligations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Article 1 of CRC defines children as persons below the age of 18.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This means that children between the ages of 16 and 18 are not covered by the protection under CYPA.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Children between 16 and 18 years old are also not protected by section 29 of CYPA which protects those under 16 years old from being detained for adult offences.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This gap in our law is again not consistent with our obligations under CRC as Article 37 obliges state parties to ensure that every child up to the age of 18 is detained and separated from adults.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Consider this, at 17 years old, many of our sons and daughters are still wearing school uniforms in junior college or attending polytechnic or Institute of Technical Education.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Until they reach the age of 18, surely they could be given the full protections Singapore has signed up to provide under CRC.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: Many drug offenders are already disadvantaged socio-economically − troubled backgrounds, disrupted lives.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: I have met some at my Meet-the-People Sessions in my constituency and what they tell me is that it is not just a stigma that gets in the way of returning to society meaningfully but also the skills gaps, especially when industry and job practices change during the years of incarceration.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: So, this is why, in prison, rehabilitation must continue to include skills training to help employability upon release.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: In particular, what efforts are being made to improve the skills of our fellow Singaporeans who are in prison, so that they can have better odds of finding a job and reintegrating into society upon release?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In August last year, during the debate on the SkillsFuture Singapore Agency Bill, I asked the Minister for Education to consider how to push training and education content via, say, an e-learning platform to those serving prison sentences.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am raising this again and I would like to highlight two statistics from the Singapore Prison Service.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why are fewer inmates getting access to training programmes?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can we consider different ways of enabling training for prisoners?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can SkillsFuture support our prisons by providing more platforms for education and training content for our inmates?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Pushing training to prisoners will facilitate the rehabilitation process help make them productive workers and even, possibly, entrepreneurs in their future.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: SkillsFuture can be used for e-learning or for training conducted within incarceration or detention premises.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the United States (US), we hear examples of prisoners obtaining university degrees while serving their sentences.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As SPS says, serving time should never be a waste of time.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Louis Ng, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I visited a Drug Rehabilitation Centre (DRC) and saw first-hand the work our Captains of Life do.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A significant focus of the rehabilitation process is to ensure that inmates secure a job when they are released.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I feel an equally important factor is whether they have family support when they are released.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is a clear sign that inmates lack family support and this is a problem that might have existed prior to their drug problem.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Strained family ties were perhaps one of the reasons they consumed drugs in the first place.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to address the root of the problem.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share what plans it has to strengthen family bonds during rehabilitation?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can we provide more classes on parenting, better communication with spouses and other such classes?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can we strengthen the current family programme, especially the joint session component?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I recently watched a very touching video of children of prisoners reuniting with their fathers behind bars for a day in a US prison.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I watched fathers in tears as they realised how much they missed their children and perhaps how their actions have hurt their children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I saw in the eyes of the fathers the resolve to be rehabilitated so that they can spend not just one day but the rest of their lives with their children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And I also saw what that one day meant for the children as, ultimately, they are the real victims.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I strongly feel we should introduce this programme in our prisons.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With stronger family bonds, a prisoner's rehabilitation process will be more effective.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Minister consider piloting this programme in our prisons?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have seen too many residents whose spouses are repeatedly incarcerated and how their families have been torn apart.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A key part of the rehabilitation has to be rebuilding these bonds.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As we navigate the uncertain times ahead and the future economy, we must always remember the vulnerable in our community and ensure that there are continued efforts to support them.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: One group that we should not lose sight of are those incarcerated and their families.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I believe it is important to continue ensuring that there are proper rehabilitation and support upon release from prison so that they can continue living their lives and participate in the future economy just like everyone else.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Difficulties in getting a job or stable income in a challenging economy can contribute towards some segments of the community succumbing to committing a crime, drug abuse or re-offend.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In this regard, I believe it is important to review the efforts in tackling offending, re-offending and drug abuse.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We should look at these holistically and see if there can be collaborations and partnerships with community organisations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Within the Malay/Muslim community, we see organisations, such as Pertapis and Jamiyah, supporting this effort.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: More can be done to involve some Malay/Muslim organisations in helping individuals and families in this area.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It is a matter of concern and we should be concerned.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The method of obtaining drugs has also changed.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Most alarmingly, the accessibility of the Internet has been exploited by drug traffickers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In light of these recent developments, what measures are MHA and the Central Narcotics Bureau (CNB) taking action to deter the supply of drugs into Singapore?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: What percentage of the total prison population are serving sentences for drug-related offences?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In order to tackle the drug problem holistically, rehabilitation is also vital.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: After the drug abusers are put into DRCs, what measures are taken to rehabilitate them with the mind to reduce recidivism rates?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: When a drug offender is incarcerated, it is a double tragedy − one life poisoned by drugs and drug culture; the family affected, too, especially the children.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: Is there a higher risk of intergenerational offending or becoming incarcerated, too, all things being equal?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: And how can we prevent a cycle of tragedy?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: Going upstream, we see that, in the West, there is an emerging movement to sugar-coat the drug problem.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: And with globalisation, the drug culture can easily spread, including to our shores.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: How do we inoculate our young Singaporeans at an earlier age so that they do not pick up the habit, so that they resist peer pressure and "fake news"?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: Among offenders, what is the average age of starting getting younger?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: And how can we prevent the problem from taking root in our schools and educate our young?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While violent crimes, robberies and theft have been trending downwards, cybercrime is increasing.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As more of our interactions and transactions go online, so do criminals.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Cyberattackers stealing money, information and data are costing individuals and companies here millions of dollars a year.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Millions more are lost through e-commerce cheating, online scams and ransomware.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Internet also facilitates transactions of illegal goods and services.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Vice activities are also increasingly being coordinated online.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Even recruitment by terrorists is also being conducted online.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will MHA leverage technology to transform frontline operations so that our Police Officers can react to security breaches and emergencies quickly?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What measures are in place to help the Home Team stay updated and equipped to cope with new security challenges and increasing demand?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Ministry consider increasing recruitment to boost our ability to deal with security crises?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Our crime rates continue to be low and responses to emergency calls remained prompt.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These are commendable achievements in the face of increasing threats to peace and security globally.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Of course, the heavy responsibility of protecting Singapore does not and should not rest on the Ministry and the Home Team alone.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We must recognise that this is a collective responsibility which requires the combined effort of all of us who call Singapore our home.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Ministry nonetheless has to take the leading role in coordinating this effort.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Apart from what has already been done, how does the Ministry propose to further strengthen its partnership with the community in the combat against crime, corruption and terrorism?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Desmond Choo, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The security landscape today is more uncertain and complex than ever.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, we face tremendous manpower constraints while ever more resources are needed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need to especially up our ingenuity when resources are thin.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need to operate differently and maximise technology to free up our precious manpower resources for more critical, on-the-ground work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Home Team has embarked on a transformation journey.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And what are the challenges to be tackled in this journey?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In this transformation, I envisage building up a new Home Team unit comprising officers recruited and trained from Day 1 to tackle threats in an integrated manner.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Crimes of the future will be more complex and will cut across traditional agency domains.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These officers become the links across our current agencies, facilitating whole-of-Home Team work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is also critical to have an integrated interagency training and operations command.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There is a greater need for cross and networked sensing to pre-empt threats and we must be nimble in tackling new and evolving threats.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How can we train and equip for such sensing capabilities?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Next, use technology and streamline our work processes to take administrative work away from our officers whose best work are out on the streets and on the frontline.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There is a need to review their retirement age to retain this valuable resource.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must also use technology to help our older officers work longer and more productively.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: An enlarged civilian scheme, akin to the Singapore Armed Forces' (SAF's) Military Expert scheme, will buttress competencies in the Home Team.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I had the privilege of serving with some of the most dedicated and professional full-time national servicemen (NSFs) and NSmen.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is good news for Home Team officers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In view of their outstanding contribution to Singapore and patriotism, I would like to know how the Ministry had recognised or intend to honour our Home Team NSFs and NSmen.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: At a time when security demands are escalating, every NSF and NSman count.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How can the Ministry better equip, train and deploy our officers?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many NSmen continue to want to play key roles in protecting our homeland.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I encourage the Ministry to leverage the professional expertise of our NSmen.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, many of our NSmen go on to become cybersecurity experts, financial experts or lawyers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They would be better served in continuing similar roles or training positions during their reservist.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can also be innovative in our deployment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can the Ministry consider having NSmen to sign up for non-security sensitive projects that NSmen can sign up for, much like an MHA version of upwork.com?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There is also a group of highly trained ex-regulars who can be grouped together for more involved Home Team projects.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While our NSFs serve the nation wholeheartedly, we should also help them embark on their careers post-NS.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can they also be provided with grants to upgrade themselves while serving their NS?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our Home Team NSFs and NSMen from the Home Team have served with distinction.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They are an indispensable part of our security blanket.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Let us continue to develop them into a force to be reckoned with.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Christopher de Souza, please take your three cuts together.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Would MHA provide an update on the efficacy of the remote gambling regulatory regime, in particular, whether the number of problem gamblers has increased or decreased following the introduction of the exempted operator regime?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Would MHA also provide the clamping down of illegal gambling through the recent regulatory framework?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: These parents are of the view that their children were molested.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I see the anguish in their eyes and the concern they have for their children.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: One of the main desires of these parents is for the Police to accord priority to these cases and conclude the investigations as fast as they can.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Parliament must also support the Home Team in ensuring that a strong message is sent to the culprits or potential culprits that society does not condone preying on innocent children.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Each cybercrime leaves the victim in a highly vulnerable state.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: As there is a need to remain vigilant against all forms of cybercrime, would MHA kindly provide this House an update on (a) its recent and upcoming initiatives to enjoin Singaporeans to battle cybercrime; and (b) what has been done to minimise the incidence of cybercrime and mitigate its effects?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, the fundamentals of law and order in Singapore are very strong.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That report studied the public's sense of safety and the public's confidence in the Police Force.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In that context, let me share with Members a Public Perception Survey that the Police conducted last year, the results of which came to me yesterday.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The results will put in context the general discussion on Public Service.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The top three reasons were low crime rates, more Police around and fast response to crimes.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These again give the context to what most people think.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If you think about it, 93% feel safe at night in a public space.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You will not get this result anywhere in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: New Zealand and Hong Kong, also known for good safety, carried out their own surveys.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They had 75% of people feeling safe at night.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If you go to other first-world cities, I suspect the figures will be much less and, in some cities, you will find much less than 50%.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Almost half of the public said that installation of Police Cameras at housing estates made them feel safer.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: An incredible number of the public hold the Police in high regard.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Ninety percent believe that the Police are ready to deal with any major law and order incidents and are well-prepared to respond to future security needs.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, if we ignore some of the artificially created online attacks on the Police, this is what people on the ground really believe, as opposed to Members coming here and trying to make it out that people say this and people say that and trying to create the impression that the majority believe it.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have no doubt some people believe and I have no doubt that Members are honest when they put it out.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Eight-eight percent felt that the Police provide a high quality of service.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: All of this reflects the extraordinary level of faith and trust Singaporeans have in the Police Force.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have no doubt that the same goes for the other Home Team departments.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I believe, for example, the Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) ranks very high in the people's assessment.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Many law enforcement agencies around the world will envy this.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: All of these have been possible because of several factors.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But a key and critical factor is the immense dedication and commitment of our Home Team officers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This is a survey on the Police Force but, at the broader level, it also gives a perspective to the discussions about the Public Service.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Singapore is where it is today because of three key reasons: excellent political leadership, excellent Public Service and excellent quality of our people who are extraordinarily capable.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If any one of these factors were absent, we would be in a very different position.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I can understand the frustration of Members in individual cases.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They arise for a number of reasons, for example, structural reasons, interagency issues.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But in perspective, these cases are the exception and not the rule.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In a large majority of cases, our public servants are outstanding, dedicated.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They go well beyond the call of duty and serve with heart.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And I know the Members who spoke share this view.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I spoke with Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and Mr Louis Ng and they confirmed this to me.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And Nominated Member Kuik Shiao-Yin has made a Facebook post setting out her thinking along these lines.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is, therefore, good to see the position in context.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Without an outstanding Public Service, we would not be here.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And without an outstanding Public Service, we would not get to where we want to be.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Many things go right, so we do not think about them.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Public Service works very hard so that the rest of us can go about our lives seamlessly.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In the public perception survey I mentioned earlier, 4% felt less secure compared to two years ago.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Of those who felt less secure, almost half attributed this to the threat of a terror attack.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Terrorism remains a key concern of the public, not only for those who felt less secure, but also those who felt secure but felt that the Home Team will easily handle it.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza and Dr Tan Wu Meng asked about the threat situation in respect of terrorism.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Islamic State in Iraq and Syria (ISIS)-related attacks were carried out in Indonesia and Malaysia last year.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The southern region of the Philippines may become an ISIS province or wilayat.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It has experienced a wave of terrorism-related attacks.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Most recently, on Sunday, a German was beheaded by the Abu Sayaaf Group.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: ISIS seems to be concentrating on the Southern Philippines.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The area can attract would-be terrorists from the region and become a safe haven to trained terrorists who can then come back to harm us.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Home Team has taken significant efforts to strengthen our computed tomography capabilities in 2016.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Christopher de Souza and Dr Tan Wu Meng asked for an update on this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, we launched the Police Emergency Response Teams (ERTs).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They patrol public places, such as malls and stadiums.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They talk to building owners and operators and they familiarise themselves with their operating environment and are trained to respond swiftly to neutralise threats.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Two, we sharpened our operational preparedness with major public exercises.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It tested the island-wide response of Home Team and SAF officers for terror threats.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Three, we enhanced our Police Camera coverage and video analytics capabilities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We completed the installation of Police Cameras in all 10,000 HDB blocks and multi-storey car parks under Police Cameras (PolCam) 1.0.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have started installing cameras in public areas − towns and neighbourhood centres and hawker centres.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will also develop video analytics capabilities from 2018 onwards and we will continue to strengthen our capabilities through 2017.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Amongst these steps, I will share two examples.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One, the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA) has started to enrol iris images.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This will help ICA more accurately verify a person's identity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For travellers, if they face difficulties with fingerprints, they can still do self-clearance, as long as their iris matches.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Two, to further enhance our frontline response capabilities, the Police plan to equip frontline officers with pistols.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Pistols will give our officers better firepower, compared to revolvers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They have up to three times more ammunition.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On dealing with terrorists, our position is that we will deal with anyone who engages in conduct that is potentially a trigger for terrorism.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Otherwise, the person may be counselled or placed on a Restriction Order.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: ISA allows us to do this and that has helped avoid what has happened in other places.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: According to media reports, he is a British citizen.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 2001, he was picked up by American forces in Afghanistan.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 2004, he was released without charge and repatriated to the United Kingdom (UK).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He launched a claim against the UK government and was reportedly awarded a million pounds.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 2014, he left the UK to join ISIS in Syria.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Last month, he reportedly carried out a suicide bomb attack in Mosul.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is much debate and concern within the UK whether the government's compensation was used to fund ISIS.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is not a question of whether the UK approach was right or wrong.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Each country has got to decide its own approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it is basically a question of how much risk you are prepared to take with such people.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We believe people in our society will not want to allow this to happen here.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In Singapore, Jamal would have been detained under ISA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The second example is Anis Amri, the Tunisian truck driver, who drove a truck into the Berlin Christmas Market last December.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Between 2011 and 2014, he served a four-year prison sentence in Sicily for several crimes, including arson.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He visited radical mosques, mingled with extremist preachers and was linked to extremist networks.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The German authorities had him on their radar.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But the laws did not allow the authorities to pre-emptively arrest him or produce him in court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Unable to find sufficient evidence as required by them, the monitoring stopped in September 2016.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The state police chief said that they had "exhausted all legal powers to the limit to ward off potential dangers".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Three months after the monitoring stopped, in December, the Christmas attack took place.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We should not reach that stage in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The trade-off for us is between taking a greater risk or intervening earlier.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And my view is we must be able to intervene early and decisively.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The imam is reported to have quoted a verse from the Quran and he seems to have said, I quote, "God grant us victory over Jews and Christians", amongst other things.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And he seems to have repeated it and said it more than once.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will know the context of what he said once the investigations have finished.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At this stage, let me say this to make clear the Government's position.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the imam had referred to the phrase to say, for example, that such phrases can promote ill-will, hatred, enmity or violence against other communities and that this is not acceptable in a multi-religious society, then there can be no objection.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But if he had said that Jews and Christians should be defeated and for God to grant Muslim brothers victory over them, to make that very point, then that is completely unacceptable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if any Member disagrees, I welcome him or her to stand up and clarify.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Government has taken a strict position when Muslims have been attacked.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: People have been charged and sent to jail.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have to be fair to the imam.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Thus, I have set out the position in the broadest possible way, outlining the Government's position so that everyone is clear where, as a matter of principle, the Government stands on these issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Even as we make clear that we do not fully know the exact context in which the imam spoke, the Government's position has to be made clear because matters like these have the potential to escalate with people jumping in, opinions being formed, hardened along religious lines.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A National University of Singapore (NUS) academic, Khairudin Aljunied, has come out to criticise the individual who made public what the imam has said.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Aljunied has encouraged vilification of that individual.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Looking at what Mr Khairudin Aljunied has said, he seems to suggest that it is okay for the imam to say that Jews and Christians should be defeated.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He assumes that the imam intended to mean that and Mr Khairudin Aljunied sees nothing wrong with that, even if the imam had intended the meaning of his words.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Khairudin Aljunied's position and actions are quite unacceptable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He has jumped into this without verifying the facts and without checking the context.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He supports a position that is quite contrary to the norms, values and laws in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Police will look into the issues and the conduct of everyone involved quite thoroughly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When such issues arise, it is best that parties referred it to the Police.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The objective is to have at least one Prepared Citizen in every household who knows how to recognise and report suspicious behaviour and items, protect their family and themselves and keep calm and reach out to others in times of crisis.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: To achieve this, we have embarked on an extensive outreach effort.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Patrick Tay, Dr Tan Wu Meng and Ms Rahayu Mahzam asked for an update.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our Home Team officers, NSmen, volunteers and grassroots leaders have been conducting house visits.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: During these visits, they explain to residents how they should respond in the event of an attack and encourage residents to participate in SGSecure programmes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will push ahead with our efforts in 2017.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We also launched the "SGSecure in the Neighbourhood" programme.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We revamped the Emergency Preparedness (EP) Day in 2016.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Residents learn skills, such as cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and first aid.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will expand our outreach efforts to workplaces in 2017.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will train public officers in SGSecure skills.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will partner the Ministry of Manpower, the National Trades Union Congress and the Singapore Business Federation to engage unions and businesses.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will have SGSecure briefings and conferences, customised EP Days; and CT seminars for industries, such as the security, manufacturing and hospitality sectors.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We urge companies to come forward and join us.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This year, we will also focus on strengthening community cohesion and resilience.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We need to make sure our community comes together as one united people after an attack.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Rahayu Mahzam spoke about how we can improve the training of our community leaders to respond after an attack.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have begun to pilot the Crisis Response Exercises (CRX) within the constituencies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: CRX will involve C2E committee members, IRCC representatives and other community stakeholders in the neighbourhood, such as schools and merchant associations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They will work together in a simulated attack scenario to assist the community after an attack and to manage potential communal tensions and restore social cohesion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, our Home Team psychologists will partner the People's Association.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Together with psychologists from the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) and the Institute of Mental Health (IMH), they will support and train grassroots leaders to provide swift and effective psychological first aid to affected residents after an attack.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our NSmen play an important role in SGSecure and they can be active responders in emergencies, whether on or off their NS duties.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some of our NSmen have also stepped forward to mobilise their communities, for example, SCDF NS Commander Lieutenant-Colonel (LTC) (NS) Raizan bin Abdul Razak.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He works with his local grassroots at Tampines West to raise awareness of the terrorism threat and rallies fellow SCDF NSmen to promote SGSecure in their neighbourhoods and social circles.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A series of events and initiatives that have been lined up to recognise the importance of contributions of our NSmen made towards nation-building.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will continue to count on them also in the fight against terrorism.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The New York Times ran an article in January this year on what it called the "Killer Drug Epidemic" in the US.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Across the US, cheap smuggled heroin is "handed out like candy".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The 33,000 figure is higher than the number killed due to pure gun homicide.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Babies are now being born with drug dependency.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Entire neighbourhoods are affected and there is little hope for young people in these neighbourhoods.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The article told the story of a young 24-year-old girl who was doing well in school.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She got addicted, went in and out of rehabilitation eight times, still unsuccessful.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And to pay for her drugs, she lied to her family, pawned her mother's jewellery and went into prostitution.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Countless others die, either through drugs or through drug-related violence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are hundreds of thousands of such examples across the world.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our approach − we have a tough legal framework against traffickers and abusers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We carry out intensive efforts to educate Singaporeans on the dangers of drug abuse, and all this is complemented by comprehensive rehabilitation measures.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Economist ran a major article in January this year.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It said that Asia's harsh anti-drug policies are falling out of step with the rest of the world.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It criticised these policies as needlessly severe and probably ineffective.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It caveated that by saying that this is because we are small, have secure borders, little corruption, effective anti-drug education and laws that allow searches without warrants and detention without trial.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Apart from our size, none of the other factors happen by themselves.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They are the result of our policies and many years of hard work.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is strong public support, both for our tough laws and our approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Singapore's example demonstrates that the vision of a drug-resistant society is not impossible with the right policies properly executed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The same Economist article referred to me as "Singapore's Fearsome Law and Home Affairs Minister" and it quoted my speech at the 2016 UN General Assembly, where I said, "Show us a model that works better, that delivers a better outcome for citizens and we will consider changing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If that cannot be done, then don't ask us to change." I do not accept the description "fearsome".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I will not flinch from taking a position in Singapore and outside Singapore that I believe is in the interest of our people.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In this context, let me also put to rest one other myth.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Recently, there have been some suggestions that international pressure will cause us to deviate from our policies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the death penalty was referred to in that context.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A penalty will be in the books if we believe it to be right, and it will be removed if we believe that removal is the right thing to do, and not because of any international pressure.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The challenge of keeping Singapore drug-free is increasing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, there are growing threats from the region.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Southeast Asia continues to be a major market and producer of illicit drugs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The trafficking of ice and heroin in the region generates over US$32 billion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This lucrative black market has attracted criminal syndicates from Africa, Iran, South Asia, Mexico and, of course, China.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Singapore will be overrun by these syndicates, if we do not take a tough approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will continue to partner them as we work towards a united position in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The second challenge is that the number of new drug abusers in Singapore has increased.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A survey conducted by the National Council Against Drug Abuse in 2016 found that young people below the age of 30 were more open-minded towards drugs, as compared to a similar 2013 survey.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng also raised similar concerns.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This problem is compounded by the rise in online drug availability.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Online black market sites allow users to buy drugs anonymously.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Drugs are couriered in small parcels, unmarked, innocuous-looking and difficult to track.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Many of us may think that only young people from low-income households are vulnerable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But the Task Force on Youths and Drugs commissioned a study in 2014.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It found that most young cannabis abusers come from either middle or high socio-economic backgrounds.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Central Narcotics Bureau (CNB) will take active measures, together with our community partners, to tackle this concern.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Third, there is increasing international pressure to adopt a softer "harm reduction" approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have to remain steadfast in our resolve to keep Singapore drug-free.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will continue to work with our partners, at regional and international platforms, to safeguard our position.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I will cover three aspects of this transformation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, we are ramping up the use of technology to better combat crime, secure our borders and save lives.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Second, we are further integrating the Home Team's operations, so that we can more effectively deal with evolving and complex threats.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Third, we are strengthening the Home Team's partnerships with the community, because everyone has a stake in keeping Singapore safe and secure.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh and Mr Desmond Choo spoke about leveraging technology.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are doing so across the whole spectrum of our operations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: One example is the use of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They give our officers a bird's-eye view of the situation and allow them to make better ground decisions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have begun to deploy UAVs to support Police and SCDF operations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For instance, in the Tuas View Circuit fire just last week, after the fire was extinguished, the UAV located hotspots in the large area which were otherwise out of sight from the firefighters.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This allowed SCDF to act quickly and prevent the hotspots from re-igniting the fire.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will train our officers to use technology and help them adapt to new ways of working.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Indeed, our people are central to our transformation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Officers will deepen their skills and master new ones.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will redesign jobs as new technologies are introduced.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: One example is ICA's automated self-clearance lanes for motorbikes at our land checkpoints.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: ICA officers who no longer have to man the counters as a result can now be trained and redeployed to detect suspicious travellers and manage incidents on the ground.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Desmond Choo also highlighted the need for Home Team departments to work together.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have taken steps to further integrate Home Team operations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Murali Pillai spoke about the importance of the Home Team partnering the community, and I agree.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: An active citizenry that is invested in the safety and security of Singapore is essential to the Home Team's work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have, therefore, stepped up efforts to strengthen partnerships between the Home Team and the community.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: (In Mandarin):   The Save-a-Life initiative by SCDF seeks to increase peoples' awareness of first aid and build a nation of lifesavers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Trained community responders can become first aiders to provide initial response to out-of-hospital cardiac arrest cases.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will scale up community involvement in three ways.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, we will equip citizens with the skills to help those who suffer a cardiac arrest.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In the coming years, we hope to train more than 24,000 residents, or about 300 residents, per constituency.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Second, we will install more AEDs across Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Currently, there are close to 460 AEDs installed in eight constituencies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Third, we still need to find a way to bring help to persons in need.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is where the SCDF's myResponder app comes in.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The app alerts its users if there is a report of somebody suffering from cardiac arrest nearby.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I urge more people to learn CPR-AED, download and use the myResponder app, and be part of our life-saving force.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will amend the Public Order Act to require certain events to put in place security measures.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will also introduce a Bill to enact a new Infrastructure Protection Act.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In imposing these requirements, we are mindful of the potential impact on businesses.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will take a practical approach so as to keep the cost of such measures reasonable.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is a cost which terrorism has imposed on society as a whole.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Government has borne a significant share of this cost.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Communities have been roped in to play their part through SGSecure, and we seek the business community's understanding that these measures are necessary as a shared effort to keep Singapore and Singaporeans safe.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Another important partner in ensuring Singapore's safety and security is the Private Security Industry.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The quality of our private security agencies has improved.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Progressive Wage Model has also laid the foundation to raise the skills, wages and productivity of our security officers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To build on these developments, MHA will work with the tripartite partners to develop an Industry Transformation Map (ITM) for the Private Security Industry, with a strong focus on innovation and technology, as well as the upgrading of jobs and skills of our officers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Zainal Sapari highlighted areas for review in the Security Agencies Grading Exercise (SAGE).

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In working on the ITMs, we will certainly take his comments and suggestions into account.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Ms Sylvia Lim raised some concerns about having foreigners as APOs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The reality is that there is a shortage of APOs, as Ms Sylvia Lim also acknowledges.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It has not been possible for the Auxiliary Police Forces to recruit only Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, we have to decide what to do.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They supplement our Singaporean APOs to meet our security needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They are properly screened to ensure that they are suitable for security work and we also make careful assessments with regard to where they are deployed, and this is reviewed from time to time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have not heard of a more effective proposal.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Anytime we give weapons to people, there is that risk.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have had isolated cases of both local and foreign APOs misusing their arms.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But we have to arm our officers with weapons, if the risk assessment and operational needs so require, so that they can carry out their tasks and protect our installations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Not doing so may compromise our security even more.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have to recognise and manage the risks through screening, training and supervision, whether it is an APO of Singaporean or foreign origin who is equipped with arms.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our priority is still to increase the number of Singaporean APOs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Singaporeans APOs are employed on better terms than foreigners, and the Auxiliary Police Forces have stepped up efforts to attract more Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I will now respond to other questions from Members.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked for an update on cybercrime.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Cybercrime continues to grow in scale and complexity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Under the plan, we have stepped up efforts to raise public awareness, as prevention remains key.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Police's Scam Alert portal educates members of the public on the latest scams and we launched an Anti-Scam Helpline in November last year for members of public who wish to seek advice on potential scam situations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are also enhancing our agencies' capabilities and strengthening our legislation, so that we remain effective in fighting cybercrime.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Christopher de Souza also asked for an update on the exempt operator regime under the Remote Gambling Act.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is too early to draw conclusions on the impact of the regime on problem gambling.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: MHA and MSF will continue to monitor the situation and adjust our regulation, if necessary.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The National Council on Problem Gambling (NCPG) has also stepped up public education and outreach on problem gambling.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Ms Sylvia Lim also asked about how the rights of the accused are safeguarded during Police investigations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: She also made observations on the time taken for Police investigations, in the context of people who hold vocational licences.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: When a Police report is lodged and there is a prima facie case, the Police have a duty to investigate.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Investigations will invariably impact those involved, such as accused persons, victims and witnesses, and we understand this.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Regulatory agencies that issue licences, including vocational licences, have a responsibility to consider the potential risks to the public and to assess whether there is a need to suspend or revoke those licences.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In the case of vocational driving licences, the suspension or revocation is determined by the Land Transport Authority.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They consider each case and whether the commuter's safety is at risk.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If this creates hardship, then we should immediately refer these individuals to social support agencies so that they get assistance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I assure the Member that the Police will conduct investigations as speedily as possible.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Although they try to expedite investigations, they also require sufficient time to conduct a thorough and fair investigation, and some cases will take longer to investigate.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This applies as well for investigations into alleged sexual abuse against minors, which Mr Christopher de Souza asked about.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Police treat such cases with great urgency.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But speed should not come at the expense of due process, diligence and sensitivity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Utmost care is taken to support child victims during investigations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, investigations are carried out in private consultation rooms designed to provide a safe and comfortable environment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Investigation officers are specially trained to use interviewing techniques sensitive to the welfare and emotional state of the child.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are also working with agencies to reduce the number of times a victim has to recount his or her experience to different parties.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: On providing early access to counsel, we need to be fair to the accused, but also to the victims and to society as a whole.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We should protect the rights of the accused without prejudicing the rights of the victims and the safety and security of society.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have, therefore, taken the approach of granting access to counsel within a reasonable time after investigations begin.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Ms Sylvia Lim also asked about the status of the video recording of interviews (VRI) pilot.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: My Minister had spoken about it last year.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For youths between 16 and 18 years old facing criminal charges, which Ms Sylvia Lim spoke about, there are various protective measures in place.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Offenders in this age group are usually dealt with by the Community Court, which is committed to restorative justice and rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These offenders could be asked to undergo family conferences or offender-victim mediations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Youths below 19 years old who commit minor offences can also be diverted from prosecution in Court to community-based rehabilitation programmes, such as the Guidance Programme and Enhanced Streetwise Programme.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Ms Sylvia Lim also asked whether parents could be allowed to be Appropriate Adults.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There is the risk that some persons related to the young suspect would face difficulties staying neutral during the interview.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Therefore, we prefer a neutral third-party, with no direct interest, to be the Appropriate Adult.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This will achieve the objective of providing emotional support to young suspects without unduly interfering with the investigation process.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Together, we will continue to keep Singapore safe and secure.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked about our drug situation and the strategies to combat this trend.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: The overall drug abuse situation in Singapore is under control.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Therefore, we cannot take our foot off the pedal in the fight against drugs.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Even with our tough drug laws and active enforcement, we remain vulnerable to the global and regional drug trade.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Minister Shanmugam highlighted the situation in the Golden Triangle, as well as the cross-border drug syndicate activities.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We must continue to strengthen our enforcement efforts and regional cooperation.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: CNB works closely with its foreign partners to target syndicates which attempt to supply drugs to Singapore.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: For example, last December, CNB and the Malaysian Narcotics Crime Investigation Department (NCID) coordinated operations to successfully nab an elusive Malaysian and his associates who were supplying a sizeable amount of drugs into Singapore.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: At the same time, we need to reduce demand and step up preventive drug education so that Singaporeans know the dangers of drugs.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng highlighted the growing movement overseas to sugar-coat the drug problem.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Our youths are not immune from this influence.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: On the Internet, our youths see drugs being glamourised.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: They read about the legalisation of cannabis overseas and they hear that drugs like cannabis are less harmful and addictive.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: The World Health Organization has also compiled research which found that regular cannabis users were more likely to take other drugs like heroin and cocaine.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: To better engage youths and extend outreach, CNB has developed a multi-pronged strategy.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: First, CNB has been increasing their social media presence and they have produced videos to convey accurate information on the harms of drugs.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: These are shared online, as well as during drug prevention talks and roadshows.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Second, CNB is piloting a new initiative to establish positive "influencers" in peer circles.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Youths from the Institutes of Technical Education, polytechnics and universities have signed up for the pilot of an Anti-Drug Advocate (ADA) Programme.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: These youths will learn about the harmful effects of drugs and Singapore's drug policies.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: They will visit halfway houses and DRCs, hearing first-hand accounts from ex-abusers on how hard it is to kick the drug habit.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: These youths will see what is really at stake if they try drugs.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We hope the experience will encourage them to start their own initiatives to spread the anti-drug message to their friends.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We need more people to step forward to spread the anti-drug message.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Prevention is our first line of defence, and a key part of the battle is won if we keep our people away from drugs.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: However, when someone starts to abuse drugs, we must help them to stop.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: And it is vital that we curb the vicious cycle of re-offending and prevent the spread of drug to non-abusers.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Last year, CNB arrested a man for drug trafficking.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: He got them addicted and even supplied their habit.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We share Dr Tan Wu Meng's concern on the impact of drug abuse on the family.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: If we do not succeed rehabilitating offenders, their families, including their children, may end up becoming victims or offenders.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Curbing intergenerational offending starts upstream, and this applies to both drug abuse and crime.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: This is an area which we are working with other agencies to better understand and tackle.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Inmates are assessed for their risk of re-offending and severity of drug abuse and, depending on risk levels, inmates undergo different programmes which address criminal thinking and addiction issues.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: They also undergo family support programmes, religious programmes and skills training.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: To ease their transition back into the community, they can later be emplaced in a halfway house or on home detention.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We hope these measures help inmates better reintegrate into society.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about the role of family support in rehabilitation.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Indeed, this is one of the key factors that motivates ex-offenders to rebuild their lives and to keep themselves away from re-offending.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: The SPS partners Fei Yue Family Services and Lakeside Family Services to provide structured family programmes for inmates − workshops to help better understand the impact of their crimes on their families and build their parenting and communication skills.
